headline: Mētoru is from French mètre, a doublet of メーター (mētā).
Urikire is the nominalization of the verb 売り切れる (urikireru).
Sūgaku is 数 (sū, “number”) plus 学 (-gaku, “-logy; -graphy”).
Bakuhatsu is Middle Chinese 爆發, literally “burst, explode + fly or send forth”.
Tanomoshii is from the Early Middle Japanese adjective 頼もし (tanomoshi), whose ending later lost its medial k.
Uwa is the combining form of ue, ancient upe.
Keikōtō is 蛍光 (keikō, “fluorescent”) plus 灯 (tō, “light”).
Gikai is 議 (“debate; deliberation; discussion”) plus 会 (“gathering”).
Sōzō is Middle Chinese 創造, literally “to begin + to make”.
Tōge, a mountain pass, is a sound shift from 手向け (tamuke, “tribute to a person about to depart”).
Fukisoku is 不 (fu-, “un-; non-”) plus 規則 (kisoku, “rule”).
Yuki, “bound for”, is compared on its page to Korean 행 (haeng), written with the same 行.
Denchū is 電 (den, “electric”) plus 柱 (chū, “pole”).
Sōri daijin is 総理 (“prime minister”, literally “leader”) plus 大臣 (“(senior) minister”).
Tetsudō is 鉄 (tetsu, “iron, steel”) plus 道 (dō, “way”), a calque of German Eisenbahn.
Tatsu, “to sever”, resembles Proto-Tai *tacᴰ (“to cut”), though the page offers it only as a similarity.
Nokori is the continuative stem of 残る (nokoru, “to remain”).
Makkura is 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) plus 暗 (kura, “dark”).
Nanika is 何 (nani, “what”) plus か (ka, indefinite particle).
Umai is from the Early Middle Japanese adjective うまし (umashi), its ending reshaped in two steps.
Waku is a kokuji, a Japanese-coined character: 木 plus 卆, and not a simplification of 木 plus 卒.
Mendōkusai is 面倒 (“inconvenience”) plus 臭い (“reeks of”).
Ōfuku, “round trip”, began as waupuku and lost its w along the way.
In kaiten, 回 is a daiyōji replacing 廻.
Anna contracts あの様な (ano yō na).
Ryōshi “should” be gyoshi: the ryō comes from confusion with 猟, which means hunting.
Na, “name”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *na; compare Okinawan nā.
Egaku is 絵 (e, “picture”) plus 書く (kaku, “write”): literally “to write a picture”.
Hikari is the nominalized stem of the verb 光る (hikaru, “to shine, to glitter, to gleam”).
Wasureru is from Old Japanese 忘る (wasuru), from Proto-Japonic *wasuru.
Jitai is 字 (“character”) plus 体 (“form”).
